title: Odd/Even or Half ? Entanglement Anomaly in the Bose-Hubbard model
authors: Humberto E. López-Hernández, Santiago F. Caballero-Benitez
abstract: The area law relates the bipartite entanglement entropy of a quantum many-body ground state to the size of the boundary between the subsystems, but the geometry of this boundary is rarely discussed. We inspect this in the 1D Bose-Hubbard model at fixed density by comparing four spatial bipartitions of the periodic lattice: first half, second half, even sites, and odd sites; sharing the same number of sites but differing in how the boundary is arranged. We find analytical limits with perturbation theory: in the Mott insulator the contiguous cut obeys the area lay while the alternating cut obeys a volume law $S\propto N_s$, in this sense an anomaly, and for the superfluid both cuts colapse to the binomial saturation due to delocalization of the state. We formulate these limits as a statement about the many-body problem using a generalized slave-boson approach based on mean-field with quantum fluctuations while verifying with Exact Diagonalization (ED) for small lattice sizes and Densitiy Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) simulations for $N_s\gg 1$. The slave-boson Gaussian ground state allows to compute the entanglement entropy from a reduced correlation matrix for any desired bipartition consistent with ED and DMRG results. Using slave bosons the computational cost is set by the local cutoff $n_{\max}$ rather than the Hilbert space dimension, so we can reach lattice sizes far beyond ED. Our method is capable of establishing the partition-dependent scaling laws as a many-body feature, not only a finite-size effect, in great agreement with the ED for $N_s\in[4,10]$ and DMRG for larger lattice sizes.
summary: This paper analyzes the entanglement entropy in the 1D Bose-Hubbard model by comparing different spatial bipartitions (e.g., half vs. odd/even sites). Using a slave-boson approach, the authors reveal a significant anomaly in the Mott Insulator phase where the entanglement scaling differs drastically between contiguous and alternating cuts. This highlights that entanglement structure is not solely determined by global symmetries but by the specific geometry of the boundary.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the geometry of the boundary affects the bipartite entanglement entropy in the 1D Bose-Hubbard model, comparing contiguous (half) versus alternating (odd/even) cuts.
main_result: In the Mott Insulator regime, the entanglement entropy exhibits a clear anomaly: the half cut follows the area law, while the alternating cut follows a volume law, demonstrating partition-dependent scaling.
method: The authors employ a generalized slave-boson mean-field approach, supplemented by perturbation theory, and validate results using Exact Diagonalization (ED) and DMRG simulations.
model_or_system: The system is the 1D Bose-Hubbard model on a periodic lattice, described by a Hamiltonian involving hopping ($t$) and on-site interaction ($U$). The analysis covers both Mott Insulator (MI) and Superfluid (SF) regimes.
key_observables: Bipartite entanglement entropy ($S_A$) for different spatial bipartitions (half, even/odd, single-site cuts).
important_parameters: The ratio of interaction to hopping ($U/t$), which dictates the phase (MI vs. SF), and the lattice size ($N_s$).
main_assumptions: The slave-boson approach is used to compute entanglement entropy, and the analysis relies on perturbation theory in the MI regime and mean-field approximations in the SF regime.
figures_summary: Figures compare entanglement entropy ($S_A$) across different cuts (half vs. even/odd) in the MI regime, showing the expected scaling difference, and illustrate the agreement between ED, SB, and perturbation theory results.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by comparing entanglement scaling laws for different cuts in the Bose-Hubbard model. It develops the slave-boson formalism to calculate $S_A$ for both cut types, derives analytical limits via perturbation theory in the MI phase, and verifies these findings against numerical benchmarks (ED/DMRG) across the phase diagram.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, quantitative study of entanglement structure in a fundamental quantum model relevant to ultracold atoms, showing that entanglement scaling is highly sensitive to the geometric structure of the partition, a key concept in quantum many-body physics.
